prompt: A perf stat run reports 12,673,112,480 cycles and 8,430,221,760 instructions for a loop. What is the IPC (instructions per cycle), and what does that value suggest?
choices: About 0.67 IPC — low for a superscalar core, suggesting the loop is stalling on something other than ALU throughput (likely memory)
About 1.50 IPC — typical, suggesting the loop is well-optimized and compute-bound
About 2.00 IPC — the theoretical maximum for any x86 core, suggesting peak efficiency
About 0.067 IPC — suggesting the CPU is mostly idle waiting on I/O

The chronological duration the function ran, left to right in time order
The number of threads concurrently executing that function
The depth of that function's call stack

prompt: An AVX2 __m256 register is 256 bits wide. How many 32-bit single-precision floats fit into one register, and therefore how many a single _mm256_fmadd_ps instruction processes at once?

SAXPY does 2 FLOPs per element (1 multiply, 1 add) while moving 12 bytes per element (4-byte read of x, 4-byte read-modify-write of y). After vectorizing to AVX2, instruction count dropped ~8x but wall-clock time only dropped ~2.3x, with cache-misses essentially unchanged. What explains this?
choices: The kernel's arithmetic intensity (FLOPs per byte) is low, so it's memory-bandwidth bound, not compute bound — fewer instructions don't reduce the bytes that must cross the memory bus
The compiler failed to emit a real FMA instruction, so no vectorization actually occurred
AVX2 only supports 4 lanes for single-precision floats, not 8
Vectorizing a loop always increases the cache-miss count, which offset the gains

prompt: perf stat -r 10 ./prog reruns the binary 10 times and reports mean ± stddev instead of a single elapsed-time number. Why is this preferable, consistent with the repeated-trial habit used in the Tier 2 cache-latency pointer-chasing microbenchmark?
choices: A single run can be skewed by cold caches, frequency ramp-up, first-touch page faults, and OS scheduling noise; repeated trials reveal the true variance instead of one possibly-unrepresentative sample
perf cannot compute hardware counters at all unless the command is run at least 10 times
Repeating the run increases the sampling frequency used by perf record
It disables address space layout randomization, which perf stat requires

prompt: Why does perf record -g -F 99 sample at 99 Hz instead of a round number like 100 Hz?
choices: To avoid lockstep aliasing with other periodic system activity (like a 100Hz timer tick) that could systematically bias which code gets caught in samples
99 Hz is the maximum sampling rate the Linux kernel allows for any profiler
It matches the AVX2 execution unit's internal clock divider
It caps the output file to exactly 99 bytes per sample for storage efficiency
